y-m-55-01.title: Checking whether the value we found is really a solution
y-m-55-01.topic: Checking solutions of an equation with an unknown in the denominator
y-m-55-01.goal: For an equation with an unknown in the denominator, work out under what conditions the changes in the solving process are allowed, check by putting the value found into the original expression whether it is a solution, and fix the order of the solution.
y-m-55-01.thinking.0: Finding whether each line of the solution has a hidden condition
y-m-55-01.thinking.1: Checking separately whether the value found is only a candidate or really a solution
y-m-55-01.thinking.2: Stating the conclusion ('there is no solution') together with its evidence
y-m-55-01.prereq.0: That in a fractional expression the value is not defined if the denominator is 0 (middle school level)
y-m-55-01.prereq.1: The experience of solving linear equations
y-m-55-01.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-01.s.s1.prompt: What happens if you put Hyeonu's answer x=2 directly in the place of x in the original expression x/(x−2) = 2/(x−2)?
y-m-55-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put 2 in the place of x and first calculate what the denominator x−2 becomes.
y-m-55-01.s.s1.hint.1: Work out whether a fraction has meaning when its denominator is that value.
y-m-55-01.s.s1.o.a: Both sides become the same value, so the equation holds
y-m-55-01.s.s1.r.a: You treated both sides having the same form as the same as having a value. Check the value of the denominator first.
y-m-55-01.s.s1.o.d: The left side becomes 0 and the right side becomes 1, so they differ
y-m-55-01.s.s1.r.d: You tried to treat a fraction with 0 in the denominator as some number. A value divided by 0 is not defined.
y-m-55-01.s.s1.explain: If you put in x=2, the denominator x−2 becomes 0, so neither the left side nor the right side has a defined value. So you cannot say 'both sides are equal,' and 2 is not accepted as a solution.
y-m-55-01.s.s2.prompt: Pick one wrong line in Hyeonu's solution.
y-m-55-01.s.s2.hint.0: Next to each line, write whether there is a 'condition under which you may do this.'
y-m-55-01.s.s2.hint.1: Look at for which x the expression x−2 used in line 1 becomes 0.
y-m-55-01.s.s2.line.0: Multiply both sides of x/(x−2) = 2/(x−2) by (x−2).
y-m-55-01.s.s2.line.2: Therefore the solution of the equation is x = 2.
y-m-55-01.s.s2.explain: Line 1 made a change that can be done only when x−2 is not 0, but did it without a condition. Line 3 called the value found a solution without checking whether it satisfies the original condition (the denominator is not 0). Line 2 is correct as a calculation if you follow line 1. The problem is not the calculation but that the condition that allows the change and the final check were left out.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.prompt: How many real solutions does this equation have? Also write what you would tell Hyeonu to write first when starting the solution.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.hint.0: Carry over directly, as the conclusion, the result of putting it into the original expression after the answer came out.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.hint.1: Before starting the solution, first write whether there is a value x cannot take.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my conclusion (the number of solutions) match the result of putting x=2 into the original expression?
y-m-55-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you mention the order of writing the condition 'before calculating'?
y-m-55-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about how the conclusion could be different if both sides were exactly the same expression x/(x−2)?
y-m-55-01.s.s3.model.0: x=2, which makes the denominator x−2 equal to 0, cannot be used. So if you first write the condition that x is not 2 and then solve, you get x=2, which clashes with the condition. Therefore there is no solution.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.model.1: When I put in x=2, the denominators of both sides become 0, so it doesn't work. Then there is no solution. If you write x≠2 first before multiplying, you can prevent this kind of mistake.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: A short solution stated without a table is also enough.
y-m-55-01.material: Hyunwoo solved the equation x/(x−2) = 2/(x−2). (How to read it: "x over (x minus 2) equals 2 over (x minus 2)." x is a real number.) Hyunwoo said, "x=2 is the solution. I don't think I need to check it."
y-m-55-01.s.s1.o.b: The denominator x−2 becomes 0, so the values of both sides are undefined
y-m-55-01.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that first checks whether the value of the expression exists.
y-m-55-01.s.s1.r.c: You may have mixed up the x for which the numerator is 0 with the x for which the denominator is 0. When x=2, the numerator is 2.
y-m-55-01.s.s3.model.2: There is no solution. First we must write that the value that makes x−2 equal 0 cannot be used.

y-m-55-02.title: Controlling the roots of x²+kx+4=0 with k
y-m-55-02.topic: The number and signs of the real roots of a quadratic equation
y-m-55-02.goal: Check, by making examples, that for a quadratic equation containing the letter k the number and signs of the real roots change with the value of k, and explain with numbers why a positive k does not work.
y-m-55-02.material: k is a real constant, and the solutions of the equation x²+kx+4=0 (x squared plus k times x plus 4 equals 0) are considered only among the real numbers. If you change k, the number and the signs of the real solutions change.
y-m-55-02.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the condition (two different positive real roots)
y-m-55-02.thinking.2: Explaining with numerical examples why the condition is needed
y-m-55-02.prereq.0: The meaning of the roots (solutions) of a quadratic equation and the experience of factoring expressions of the form x²+px+q (middle school level)
y-m-55-02.prereq.1: The experience of expanding the perfect square (x+2)² = x²+4x+4
y-m-55-02.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the k for which this equation has exactly one real solution.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.hint.0: Starting with small values like k = 0, 2, put a few values in for x and check whether x²+kx+4 can become 0.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what the smallest value of the expression must be for the graph to just touch the x-axis, and rewrite x²+kx+4 in the form (x+k/2)² + (…) and express that value in terms of k.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.r.a: In x²+4=0, x² would have to be negative, so there is no real solution at all. Look again at when a single solution appears.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that tries rewriting the expression in a perfect-square form.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.r.c: Like x²+2x+4 = (x+1)²+3, it is always positive, so there is no solution. A solution does not appear just because k is not 0.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that looked at a k of the opposite sign in the same way.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.r.e: It is easy to think that the larger k is, the more solutions there are. x²+8x+4=0 has two different real solutions.
y-m-55-02.s.s1.explain: If k=4, then x²+4x+4 = (x+2)², and if k=−4, then x²−4x+4 = (x−2)², so there is one solution (a repeated solution). For k=0 and k=2 there is no solution, and for k=8 there are two different solutions.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different integers k for which x²+kx+4=0 has two different positive real solutions.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one k, solve x²+kx+4=0 directly, and check whether two different solutions come out.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.hint.1: If you found the solutions, look at the signs to see whether both are positive, and if not, change the sign of k and test again.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The solutions are two different real numbers.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.fail.c2: They do not become two different real solutions. There is no solution or one solution. Look again around the boundary value.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Both solutions are not positive. Check the signs of the solutions directly.
y-m-55-02.s.s2.explain: For example, if k=−5, then x²−5x+4 = (x−1)(x−4), so the solutions are 1 and 4. For k=−4 there is one solution (2), and for k=5 the solutions are −1 and −4, both negative. To satisfy both the sign and the number, k must be less than −4.
y-m-55-02.s.s3.prompt: Why can't both solutions be positive for a positive k such as k = 5? Explain using numbers.
y-m-55-02.s.s3.hint.0: Solve x²+5x+4=0 directly with k=5 and write the signs of the two solutions.
y-m-55-02.s.s3.hint.1: Look at what the sign of each term of x²+5x+4 is if you put in only positive numbers for x.
y-m-55-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the actual solutions calculated in the numerical example I gave?
y-m-55-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say 'why it is always so when k is positive' as a reason rather than with just one example?
y-m-55-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about what happens at the boundary values like k=4 and k=−4?
y-m-55-02.s.s3.model.0: If k=5, then x²+5x+4 = (x+1)(x+4)=0, so the solutions are −1 and −4, both negative. For the solutions to be positive, k has to be negative.
y-m-55-02.s.s3.model.1: If x is positive, x², 5x, and 4 are all positive, so their sum cannot be 0. So if k is positive, there is no positive solution.
y-m-55-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explains by signs without finding the solutions directly is also valid.

y-m-55-03.title: What do we need to know about a to state the solution?
y-m-55-03.topic: The solution of a linear inequality with a letter in the coefficient
y-m-55-03.goal: Learn that if the sign of the coefficient a (and whether it is 0) is not known, the solution of the inequality ax>6 cannot be written as a single answer, and state the information needed and the solution in each case.
y-m-55-03.material: Taemin answered the solution of the inequality ax>6 ('a times x is greater than 6') as 'x>6/a.' x is a real number, and a is a real constant, but the value of a is not given in the problem (it could be positive, 0, or negative).
y-m-55-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-55-03.thinking.2: Splitting into cases and writing the solutions
y-m-55-03.prereq.0: Showing the solution of a linear inequality on a number line or with an inequality sign (middle school level)
y-m-55-03.prereq.1: The experience of learning that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number changes the direction of the inequality sign
y-m-55-03.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.prompt: To tell whether Taemin's answer is right in all cases, what is the first thing we need to know?
y-m-55-03.s.s1.hint.0: Put 2 and −2 in for a, and directly find a few x that satisfy ax>6.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the value of 6/a and compare whether the x you found all satisfy x>6/a.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.o.a: Whether a is positive, 0, or negative
y-m-55-03.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that wants to check the sign of the coefficient before writing the solution.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.o.b: Whether x is fixed as an integer or not
y-m-55-03.s.s1.r.b: The kind of x changes the form of the solution, but it has little to do with whether the direction of the inequality sign is right. Think about what the sign of the number you divide by changes.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.o.c: Whether 6 is divisible by a or not
y-m-55-03.s.s1.r.c: Whether it divides evenly is not important among the real numbers. Pay attention to what kind of number the divisor is.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.o.d: Whether x is greater or less than 0
y-m-55-03.s.s1.r.d: Knowing the sign of x can narrow the solution, but whether Taemin's expression is right depends on a.
y-m-55-03.s.s1.explain: If you divide both sides of ax>6 by a, the direction of the inequality sign differs when a is positive and when it is negative, and if a=0 you cannot divide. So the sign of a (and whether it is 0) is needed.
y-m-55-03.s.s2.prompt: Enter 2 pairs (a, x), with different values of a, that satisfy ax>6 but are not included in Taemin's answer x>6/a. (Take a to be a nonzero value.)
y-m-55-03.s.s2.hint.0: Decide one positive and one negative a, and directly find x such that ax>6.
y-m-55-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate 6/a to compare whether the x you found satisfies x>6/a, and look at which a is on the side that does not satisfy it.
y-m-55-03.s.s2.fail.c1: ax is not greater than 6. Check the product of a and x again.
y-m-55-03.s.s2.ok.c2: It is not included in Taemin's answer x>6/a. Taemin's answer is broken.
y-m-55-03.s.s2.fail.c2: This (a, x) is also included in Taemin's answer x>6/a. It does not become a counterexample. Try changing the sign of a.
y-m-55-03.s.s2.explain: For example, if a=−2, x=−4, then ax=8>6, but 6/a=−3 and x=−4 is less than −3. That is, Taemin's answer x>6/a is not right when a is negative.
y-m-55-03.s.s3.prompt: Sort out for Taemin how the solution differs depending on the value of a. Also think about and write the case a=0.
y-m-55-03.s.s3.hint.0: When a is positive, check with numbers whether the x that makes ax>6 is greater or less than 6/a.
y-m-55-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write what expression you get if you put a=0 directly into ax>6.
y-m-55-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you deal with all three cases, a positive, negative, and 0?
y-m-55-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you put one value of a into the solution you wrote and check that ax>6 holds?
y-m-55-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish the statement 'we cannot write it as one answer because there is no information' from the statement 'we can write it if we split into cases'?
y-m-55-03.s.s3.model.0: If a is positive, x>6/a; if a is negative, dividing both sides by the negative a reverses the inequality sign, so x<6/a. If a=0, it becomes 0>6, so there is no solution.
y-m-55-03.s.s3.model.1: If a>0, x>6/a; if a<0, x<6/a; if a=0, no x satisfies ax>6, so there is no solution.
y-m-55-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer organized using only inequality signs is also enough.

y-m-55-04.title: If two values are equal at two values, is it an identity?
y-m-55-04.topic: Telling an identity apart from an equation
y-m-55-04.goal: Judge how sufficient the fact that two expressions are equal at a few values is as evidence for 'it is an identity,' revise your judgment when a new value appears, and tell an equation apart from an identity.
y-m-55-04.material: Sora is putting in values for x one at a time and comparing the two expressions x²+x and 2x (x squared plus x, and 2 times x) to find out whether they are an 'identity in x' (the case where the values of the two expressions are always equal no matter what real number is put in for x).
y-m-55-04.thinking.0: Deciding how confident a judgment is from partial evidence
y-m-55-04.thinking.1: Revising a judgment when new information appears
y-m-55-04.thinking.2: Telling an equation (holds only at particular x) apart from an identity (holds for all x)
y-m-55-04.prereq.0: Calculating the value of an expression by putting a value in for the letter x (middle school level)
y-m-55-04.prereq.1: The definition that an identity in x is an equation that always holds no matter what value is put in for x
y-m-55-04.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the calculation result newly revealed at each step, choose your judgment about Sora's question. After choosing, you may change your judgment in the next step.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write briefly how much the values so far support 'it is an identity.'
y-m-55-04.s.s1.hint.1: Each time a new value appears, compare whether the earlier judgment still holds as it is.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.info: If you put in x=0, x²+x = 0 and 2x = 0, so the two values are equal.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Looking at only this result, how would you judge 'the two expressions are an identity in x'?
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The single value x=0 is just a result that 'must hold if it is an identity' and does not guarantee that it is an identity. It is natural to put off the judgment or to test other values.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: We can conclude that it is an identity
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is thinking that took being equal at one value as evidence of being equal at all values.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: They are only equal at one value, so it is too early to judge
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that recognizes there is only one piece of evidence.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We can conclude that it is not an identity
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The same value came out, so concluding right away that it is not has no basis.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: x=0 is a special value, so we put in other values before judging
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment that wants to test other values, not only a value like 0 that looks special.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.info: If you put in x=1, x²+x = 2 and 2x = 2, so again the two values are equal.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: They were equal at two values. What is your judgment now?
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Being equal at two values does not guarantee being equal for all x. Saying the possibility has grown, or simplifying the expression to check, is a good judgment.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: We can conclude that it is an identity
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is thinking that took the same result coming out twice as evidence of being equal at all values.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The possibility has grown, but we cannot conclude yet
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a judgment that raised confidence as much as the evidence increased but put off concluding.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Now it is concluded that it is not an identity
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Only equal values came out, so drawing the opposite conclusion has no basis.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Simplify x²+x−2x and work out at which x it becomes 0
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that wants to check the answer from the expression itself instead of putting in more values.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.info: If you put in x=2, x²+x = 6 and 2x = 4, so the values are different from each other.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: With this new result, what happens to your judgment?
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The values differ at x=2, so it is not an identity. Checking the calculation once is also reasonable, but the result does not change from 6 and 4.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is an identity. Because they were equal at two values
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is thinking that treated the new opposing evidence as lighter than the earlier evidence.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is not an identity. Because there is even one x where the values differ
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is the judgment that a single counterexample breaks a general claim.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Check the calculation once more before judging
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a careful judgment that checks the possibility that the counterexample is a calculation mistake.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: x=2 is a special value, so we ignore this result
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is thinking that tries to throw away evidence that conflicts with one's own judgment.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.info: Since x²+x−2x = x²−x = x(x−1), the two expressions have equal values only when x=0 or x=1.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.ask: Then what are the real solutions of the equation x²+x = 2x?
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.after: The x=0 and 1 where they were equal before are exactly the solutions of this equation. Even for the same expressions, if it 'holds only at particular x,' it is an equation, and if it 'holds for all x,' it is an identity.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.r.a: This is thinking that missed that the two values were also equal at x=0.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.r.b: This is thinking that missed that the two values were also equal at x=1.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.r.c: This is thinking that could not tell an identity apart from an equation.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.st.3.r.d: This is thinking that gathered only the x at which the two expressions become equal as the solutions.
y-m-55-04.s.s1.reflect: The fact that the values were equal at x=0 and x=1 supported 'it may be an identity,' but it was not a proof, and one x with a different value (x=2) changed the judgment. If the same expressions are equal 'only at some x,' that is a solution of an equation, and if they are equal 'for all x,' it is an identity.
y-m-55-04.s.s2.prompt: Tell Sora in one or two sentences. Write whether these two expressions are an identity, and what it means that the values were equal at x=0 and x=1.
y-m-55-04.s.s2.hint.0: Start with one sentence that uses the two values at x=2 seen above as they are.
y-m-55-04.s.s2.hint.1: Rewrite, in the language of 'equations,' the point that x=0, 1 are the x at which the two expressions become equal.
y-m-55-04.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. It is not an identity...
y-m-55-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate whether the values of the two expressions are really different at the x I gave?
y-m-55-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in the language of equations that being equal at x=0, 1 means they are 'solutions'?
y-m-55-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write 'equal only at special values' and 'equal at all values' separately?
y-m-55-04.s.s2.model.0: It is not an identity. If you put in x=2, you get 6 and 4, which differ. The values where they are equal, x=0, 1, are the solutions of the equation x²+x=2x.
y-m-55-04.s.s2.model.1: If you put 3 in for x you get 12 and 6, which differ, so it is not an identity. The 0 and 1 where the same value came out are special values where the expressions happen to become equal.
y-m-55-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that wrote 'special values' instead of the word solutions is also valid.

y-m-55-05.title: For two equations not to hold at the same time
y-m-55-05.topic: When a system of linear equations has no solution
y-m-55-05.goal: Make (a, b, c) for which the system x+2y=3, ax+by=c has no solution, and explain by the shape of the lines which relation among the coefficients decides whether there is a solution.
y-m-55-05.material: x and y are real numbers. The first equation is x+2y=3 (x plus 2y equals 3). You will decide a, b, c of the second equation ax+by=c yourself to make a system that pairs the two equations. Each equation can be thought of as a line in the coordinate plane.
y-m-55-05.thinking.0: Making several examples that fit the condition
y-m-55-05.thinking.1: Discovering a rule in the structure of the examples (the ratio of coefficients)
y-m-55-05.thinking.2: Telling apart that there is one more case (the lines overlap)
y-m-55-05.prereq.0: That the solutions of a linear equation with two unknowns, ax+by=c, form a line in the coordinate plane (middle school level)
y-m-55-05.prereq.1: The solution of a system of equations = the (x, y) that satisfies both equations at the same time
y-m-55-05.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.prompt: If you choose the second equation to be 2x+4y=7, what happens to the solution of the system x+2y=3, 2x+4y=7?
y-m-55-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the expression you get by doubling both sides of the first equation and compare its left side with the second equation.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.hint.1: When the left sides are the same but the right sides are different, work out whether there can be x, y that satisfy both equations at the same time.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.o.a: x=1, y=1 is the one solution
y-m-55-05.s.s1.r.a: x=1, y=1 satisfies only the first equation. Think about whether you checked it in the second equation too.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.o.b: There is no (x, y) that satisfies both equations at the same time
y-m-55-05.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that compared the left sides of the two equations and found the contradiction.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.r.c: That is the conclusion for when the second equation is the same line as the first. Check whether the right side is really the same multiple.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.r.d: Two lines meet in one point, in no point, or in infinitely many points. They cannot meet in two.
y-m-55-05.s.s1.explain: Doubling both sides of the first equation gives 2x+4y=6, but the second equation is 2x+4y=7. The same 2x+4y cannot be both 6 and 7, so there is no solution.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different (a, b, c) for which x+2y=3 and ax+by=c have no solution at all. (For the equation to be a line, a must not be 0.)
y-m-55-05.s.s2.hint.0: Decide a and b while thinking about how many times the left side x+2y of the first equation gives the left side of the second equation.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.hint.1: After deciding a and b, compare c with the value you get by changing the right side 3 of the first equation by the same multiple.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.fail.c1: If a is 0, it can become an equation unrelated to x. Please use a nonzero value.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.ok.c2: In the two equations, the ratio of the coefficients of x and y is the same, so the two lines have the same slope.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The ratio of coefficients is different, so the two lines meet at one point. One solution is produced.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The right sides are different, so the two lines are in different positions.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The two equations become the same line, so there are infinitely many solutions.
y-m-55-05.s.s2.explain: For example, (2, 4, 7), (3, 6, 1), (−1, −2, 5) all have no solution. This is because the left side of the second equation is a times the left side of the first, but the right side is not a times 3.
y-m-55-05.s.s3.prompt: Pick one example you just made and explain, by the shape of the lines, why there are no x, y that satisfy both equations at the same time. Also write what changes if you set c to 3a.
y-m-55-05.s.s3.hint.0: For the example you picked, write the first equation multiplied by a and the second equation side by side and compare them.
y-m-55-05.s.s3.hint.1: Write what relation the two equations have if you change c to 3a.
y-m-55-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the example I picked, can 'the same slope, different positions' actually be confirmed?
y-m-55-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart the case with no solution and the case with infinitely many solutions?
y-m-55-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you recall that when (a, b) is different there are also cases with one solution?
y-m-55-05.s.s3.model.0: If a=2, b=4, c=7, the second equation is 2x+4y=7, and twice the first equation is 2x+4y=6. The slopes are the same but the positions are different, so the two lines are parallel and do not meet. If c=6, they become the same line and there are infinitely many solutions.
y-m-55-05.s.s3.model.1: If x+2y is 3, then 2x+4y has to be 6, but it is 7, so the two cannot hold at the same time. The slopes are the same so they are parallel, and if c is 3a the two lines overlap.
y-m-55-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that first explained in words comparing the values of the expressions is also valid.

y-m-55-06.title: Can we decide which is larger from approximations alone?
y-m-55-06.topic: Comparing the sizes of irrational numbers
y-m-55-06.goal: Learn that there are times when truncated approximations alone cannot decide the sizes of two numbers, and tell apart when you can reach a conclusion by considering the range of error and when to compare exactly without approximating.
y-m-55-06.material: A = √2+√3 (root 2 plus root 3), B = √10 (root 10). We want to find out which is larger. We do not use a calculator; instead we are given, with more digits at each step, the 'value of each number with the digits after some decimal place cut off.' We do not know how much was cut off.
y-m-55-06.thinking.0: Judging while considering the error of approximations
y-m-55-06.thinking.1: Revising judgment and confidence when more information is given
y-m-55-06.thinking.2: Confirming the same conclusion by another method
y-m-55-06.prereq.0: The meaning of square roots and approximations like √2≈1.4 (middle school level)
y-m-55-06.prereq.1: The fact that squaring two positive numbers does not change their order of size
y-m-55-06.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the information newly given at each step, choose your judgment about 'which of A and B is larger.' You may change your judgment in the next step.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write the lower and upper ends of the range each of A and B lies in.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.hint.1: After comparing whether the two ranges overlap or not, choose your judgment.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Values truncated at the first decimal place: √2 is 1.4 or more and less than 1.5, √3 is 1.7 or more and less than 1.8, and √10 is 3.1 or more and less than 3.2.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: With this information, which is larger?
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.after: A is 3.1 or more and less than 3.3, and B is 3.1 or more and less than 3.2, so the ranges overlap. This information does not let us decide.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is thinking that saw only that A's range (3.1 or more and less than 3.3) extends higher than B's. Check the part that overlaps with B's range.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is thinking that relied on the intuition that √10 of B feels larger. First check whether the two ranges overlap.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is thinking that said the two numbers are equal because the truncated values are equal. Even when truncated at the same place, the parts cut off are different.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We cannot know from this information alone
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment that worked out whether the ranges of the two numbers overlap.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What conclusion can we draw from the ranges?
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.after: A < 3.16 ≤ B, so B is larger. Even with approximations alone, if the ranges of error do not overlap, you can reach a conclusion.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A's range and B's range overlap, so we still cannot know
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is thinking that saw the numbers near 3.16 and decided they overlap. Check the difference between 'less than' and 'or more.'
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Approximations have error, so in no case can we reach a conclusion
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even with error, if the ranges do not overlap, a conclusion is possible.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.info: You can also compare without approximating. A² = (√2+√3)² = 5+2√6 and B² = 10. To compare 5+2√6 and 10, it is enough to compare 2√6 and 5, and 2√6 = √24 and 5 = √25.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.ask: Which is an appropriate evaluation of this method?
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.after: √24 < √25, so A² < B², and since both are positive, A < B. It gives the same conclusion as the approximation, but you do not need to worry about error.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.o.a: Squaring reverses the order, so B is smaller
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.r.a: This is thinking that wrongly applied to positive numbers the fact that the order reverses when squaring only for negative numbers.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.o.b: A radical remains, so we cannot compare without approximating
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.r.b: Radicals like √24 and √25 can also be compared by the numbers inside.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.o.c: They are both positive, so squaring keeps the order and they are compared exactly
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.r.c: This is thinking that checked the condition that squaring preserves the order for positive numbers.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.o.d: Squaring changes the values, so it cannot be used for comparison
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Even if the values change, if the order is the same, it can be used for comparison.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.prompt: When is it all right to compare approximations and reach a conclusion? Use the numbers of this problem at least once and write one or two sentences.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the largest possible value of A and the smallest possible value of B in this problem.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.hint.1: Using the result of comparing the two values as the evidence, write the conclusion as a sentence.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Do the numbers I wrote match the ranges in this problem?
y-m-55-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write 'compared two numbers' and 'compared taking the error into account' separately?
y-m-55-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say both when we cannot reach a conclusion and when we can?
y-m-55-06.s.s2.model.0: When comparing truncated values, you have to think about the range of error caused by the cut-off parts. This time A is 3.14 or more and less than 3.16 and B is 3.16 or more, so the ranges do not overlap and we can say B is larger.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.model.1: Up to the first decimal place both were 3.1, so we could not decide. At the second place, 3.14 and 3.16 came out, but we can settle it only after checking whether the difference 0.02 is larger than the sum of the cut-off parts.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.modelNote.1: An explanation that compares with the size of the error instead of specific ranges is also valid.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.info: The values truncated to two decimal places are known for √2 and √3: √2 is 1.41… and √3 is 1.73…. √10 is still known only to one decimal place (at least 3.1 and less than 3.2). So A has narrowed to at least 3.14 and less than 3.16.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.after: A is at least 3.14 and less than 3.16, and B is at least 3.1 and less than 3.2, so the ranges overlap. Even if only A becomes exact, if B's range is wide, you cannot decide. B also has to be known more precisely.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A is at least 3.14 and less than 3.16, and B is at least 3.1 and less than 3.2, so the ranges overlap. It cannot be decided yet
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a judgment that compared the ends of the ranges of the two numbers and checked whether they overlap.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A's range has narrowed to at least 3.14, and B is in the 3.1s, so A is greater
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: B's range is still wide, at least 3.1 and less than 3.2. Compare the largest value of A with the smallest value of B.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: B is greater. √10 feels intuitively bigger
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You should compare the ends of the ranges, not go by feeling. Check whether the two ranges overlap right now.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Check whether it can be decided if B is also given to two decimal places
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that knew that when only one side becomes exact the ranges can overlap, and decided the information needed next.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.info: √10 is now also known to two decimal places: 3.16…. Written as ranges, √2 is at least 1.41 and less than 1.42, √3 is at least 1.73 and less than 1.74, and √10 is at least 3.16 and less than 3.17. Therefore A is at least 3.14 and less than 3.16, and B is at least 3.16 and less than 3.17.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: A is less than 3.16 and B is at least 3.16, so B is greater
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a judgment that decided which is greater by comparing the ends of the ranges.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: It did not compare the upper end of A's range with the lower end of B's range.
y-m-55-06.s.s1.reflect: At first, judging by estimation alone was impossible, and when only one side had more digits, the ranges overlapped. When both sides had more digits, the ranges no longer overlapped, and a conclusion became possible. What changed the judgment was not "the numbers look plausible" but "comparing the ends of the ranges." The estimate and the exact comparison gave the same conclusion.
y-m-55-06.s.s2.model.2: If A's possible maximum, which is less than 3.16, is compared with B's minimum 3.16, and A is always smaller, we can reach a conclusion. At the first decimal place the ranges overlapped, so it did not work.

y-m-55-07.title: What will the concentration of the mixed salt water be?
y-m-55-07.topic: Concentration and setting up linear equations
y-m-55-07.goal: Find the error of simply averaging the concentrations when mixing salt water, judge what information (the amount of salt water) is further needed, and write a message that explains it to a classmate.
y-m-55-07.material: Cup A holds 100 g of salt water with concentration 10%, and cup B holds 300 g of salt water with concentration 2%. Boram found the concentration of the salt water made by mixing all the salt water of the two cups in one bowl. Assume that salt and water do not disappear or newly appear when mixing.
y-m-55-07.thinking.0: Finding an unjustified jump in a line of the solution
y-m-55-07.thinking.1: Judging the condition under which an average holds
y-m-55-07.thinking.2: Explaining the error and the correct method in a way that suits the other person
y-m-55-07.prereq.0: The meaning of concentration (%) = amount of salt ÷ amount of salt water × 100 (middle school level)
y-m-55-07.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.prompt: Pick one wrong line in Boram's solution.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.hint.0: Going from line 2 to line 3, follow where the weight of the salt was decided.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the weight of the salt in cup A and cup B separately and compare their sum with the 24 g in line 3.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.line.0: The concentration of A is 10%, and the concentration of B is 2%.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.line.1: The concentration of the mixed salt water is the middle value of the two concentrations, so (10+2)÷2=6%.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.line.2: Then the 400 g of mixed salt water contains 400×0.06=24 g of salt.
y-m-55-07.s.s1.explain: The first error happened in line 2. The amounts of the two salt waters are different, but only the concentrations were averaged. Line 3 used the 6% from line 2 as it is and got 24 g of salt, so it is wrong too. The actual salt is 10 g in A and 6 g in B, for a sum of 16 g.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.prompt: When is the concentration of two mixed salt waters the middle value of the two concentrations ((p+q)÷2)?
y-m-55-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write as an expression the weight of salt when salt waters with concentrations p% and q% are mixed in the same weight m.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.hint.1: For the case where the salt weights are the same and the case where the water weights are the same, pick numbers, calculate the mixed concentration, and compare it with the middle value.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.o.a: When the weights of salt in the two cups are the same
y-m-55-07.s.s2.r.a: Check with numbers whether the concentration becomes the average when the weights of salt are the same. You may have missed that the amounts of salt water become different.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.o.b: When the weights of water in the two cups are the same
y-m-55-07.s.s2.r.b: Having the same weight of water does not mean the total weights of the salt water are the same.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.o.c: When the difference of the two concentrations is very small
y-m-55-07.s.s2.r.c: If the difference is small they become close, but they do not become exactly equal.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.o.d: When the total weights of the salt water in the two cups are the same
y-m-55-07.s.s2.r.d: This is thinking that worked out with an expression the condition under which the average of concentrations holds.
y-m-55-07.s.s2.explain: If the weights of salt water are the same m, the mixed concentration is (m·p + m·q)÷(2m) = (p+q)÷2. When only the weights of salt are the same or only the weights of water are the same, it does not become the average.
y-m-55-07.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to send to Boram. Using numbers, write why it is not 6%, and what must be worked out to find the actual concentration in this case.
y-m-55-07.s.s3.hint.0: First write the weight of the salt in each of the two cups, and then write their sum.
y-m-55-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write the total weight of the salt water after mixing, and convert the value of the sum of the salt divided by the total weight into a percentage.
y-m-55-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the message kindly tell where it changed, without blaming Boram?
y-m-55-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do the numbers I wrote (amount of salt, total weight, concentration) connect with each other correctly?
y-m-55-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you include the statement 'if the amounts are the same, the average is right,' or, even if you did not, is the reason clear?
y-m-55-07.s.s3.model.0: Boram, you can't just average the concentrations. B has much more salt water, 300 g, so the overall concentration is closer to B's. The salt is 10 g in A and 6 g in B, a sum of 16 g, and 16 g out of 400 g is 4%.
y-m-55-07.s.s3.model.1: When you mix, the weights of salt add up and the weights of salt water add up. So you have to find (10+6)÷(100+300)×100=4%. If the amounts of the two salt waters are different, a simple average is wrong.
y-m-55-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: A message written only with expressions is also valid.

y-m-55-08.title: Which of the two points is it closer to?
y-m-55-08.topic: Reading absolute value as distance on a number line
y-m-55-08.goal: Read absolute value expressions as distances on a number line to judge the solutions of |x−1|=|x−5| and |x−1|<|x−5|, and explain that the interpretation by distance is a basis for getting the solution even without calculation.
y-m-55-08.material: On a number line, point P is at 1 and point Q is at 5. For a real number x, let point X be at x on the number line. Then |x−1| is the distance between X and P, and |x−5| is the distance between X and Q. (|x−1| is read as 'the absolute value of x minus 1.')
y-m-55-08.thinking.0: Reading an expression as the meaning of distance
y-m-55-08.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy a condition
y-m-55-08.thinking.2: Explaining by distance what the examples have in common (the boundary 3)
y-m-55-08.prereq.0: The meaning of the distance between two points on a number line and the meaning of absolute value (middle school level)
y-m-55-08.prereq.1: Calculating values like |x−1| for an integer x
y-m-55-08.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put in x=1, 5, 3, −2 and calculate |x−1| and |x−5| for each, and write them in a table.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.hint.1: Mark P and Q on the number line and estimate where a point at the same distance from both points might be.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that took the points where each absolute value becomes 0 as the solutions. Check the distance from that point to the other point.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that found the point at the same distance from the two points P and Q.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that paired up the points that are 3 away from P. Check the distance from each point to Q.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that could not find the case where one point is at the same distance from two points.
y-m-55-08.s.s1.explain: The point at the same distance from P(1) and Q(5) is the single midpoint of the two points, x=3. |3−1| = 2 = |3−5|.
y-m-55-08.s.s2.prompt: Enter 4 different integers x that satisfy |x−1| < |x−5|. (Think of it as which of P and Q the point X is closer to.)
y-m-55-08.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a few x, calculate |x−1| and |x−5| for each, and compare which is smaller.
y-m-55-08.s.s2.hint.1: Mark on the number line, separately, the x that satisfy the condition and those that do not, and look at where the boundary is.
y-m-55-08.s.s2.ok.c2: X is closer to P than to Q.
y-m-55-08.s.s2.fail.c2: X is closer to Q than to P, or at the same distance. Calculate the two distances directly and compare.
y-m-55-08.s.s2.explain: x=2, 1, 0, −3 are all closer to P. At x=3 the two distances are the same, so it does not satisfy '<.'
y-m-55-08.s.s3.prompt: The x you just made are all less than 3. Explain why using distances on the number line.
y-m-55-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write the distances from x=3 to P and to Q and compare them.
y-m-55-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write how the two distances change when x is made a little less than 3 and a little more than 3.
y-m-55-08.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If x is less than 3, ...
y-m-55-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did my explanation say why 'the midpoint of 1 and 5' is the boundary?
y-m-55-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also check which one it gets closer to for x greater than 3?
y-m-55-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether the same explanation is right even when x is not an integer (for example 2.5)?
y-m-55-08.s.s3.model.0: x has to be closer to 1, and the midpoint of 1 and 5 is 3, so points to the left of 3 are closer to 1.
y-m-55-08.s.s3.model.1: If x is 3, the distances to 1 and 5 are the same, 2, and if it gets less than 3, it gets closer to 1 and farther from 5. So every x less than 3 satisfies the condition.
y-m-55-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that directly calculated the distances at the boundary x=3 is also valid.

y-m-55-09.title: When can we write (a+b)² as a²+b²?
y-m-55-09.topic: Multiplication formulas and expanding expressions with letters
y-m-55-09.goal: Examine the error of believing that an expression checked with one or two values always holds, and make examples to check how the difference between (a+b)² and a²+b² is expressed and when it becomes 0.
y-m-55-09.material: Daeun thinks (a+b)² = a²+b². (How to read it: 'the square of a plus b equals a squared plus b squared.') When she checked by putting in a=3, b=0, (3+0)²=9 and 3²+0²=9, so it was right. Think, in words only, of a picture where a large square with side a+b is divided into one square with side a, one square with side b, and two rectangles with width a and height b.
y-m-55-09.thinking.0: Evaluating how general the example used for the check is
y-m-55-09.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the condition (the difference is 12)
y-m-55-09.thinking.2: Discovering a rule from the examples (difference = 2ab)
y-m-55-09.prereq.0: Finding the value of an expression by substituting numbers for letters (middle school level)
y-m-55-09.prereq.1: Area model: the experience of dividing a square with side a+b into one square each with sides a and b and two rectangles with width a and height b
y-m-55-09.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.prompt: How should we evaluate Daeun's check (a=3, b=0)?
y-m-55-09.s.s1.hint.0: Instead of a=3, b=0, pick a pair where a and b are both nonzero and calculate the two sides separately.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write whether the two sides are equal or different, and compare with the first check where you got only one equal value.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.o.a: It is a special case where b is 0, so it is not enough evidence that the expression is always right
y-m-55-09.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that looked at what kind of value the example used for the check was and worked out whether it is enough basis for generalizing.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.o.b: The calculation came out right, so it is sufficient evidence that the expression always holds
y-m-55-09.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that treated the calculation being right as the same as always holding.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.o.c: If you put in 0, even wrong expressions all come out right, so there is no information
y-m-55-09.s.s1.r.c: It is not that all wrong expressions look right when you put in 0. Try putting 0 into other expressions to check.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.o.d: a=3 is positive, so it always holds for positive a and b
y-m-55-09.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that talked about all positive numbers from one value. Try putting in other positive numbers to test.
y-m-55-09.s.s1.explain: If b=0, all the terms containing b disappear, so even a wrong expression can happen to be right. One example does not guarantee 'always.' This example only gives the information that there are cases where it is right.
y-m-55-09.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different pairs (a, b) for which the value of (a+b)² minus a²+b² is exactly 12. Neither a nor b may be 0.
y-m-55-09.s.s2.hint.0: Put small numbers in for a and b, calculate (a+b)² and a²+b² separately, and write the difference in a table.
y-m-55-09.s.s2.hint.1: In the table, put the difference side by side with the product of a and b and look at what relation you see.
y-m-55-09.s.s2.fail.c1: a or b is 0. Please use values that are all nonzero.
y-m-55-09.s.s2.fail.c2: (a+b)²−(a²+b²) is not 12. Calculate the two values separately and check the difference.
y-m-55-09.s.s2.explain: For example, (1, 6): 49−37=12, (2, 3): 25−13=12, (−2, −3): 25−13=12. All of them have in common that a×b=6. Pairs with a and b swapped count as the same example.
y-m-55-09.s.s3.prompt: How can the difference between (a+b)² and a²+b² be expressed with a and b? Then also write when Daeun's expression becomes right.
y-m-55-09.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the difference in the table above with a×b and write how many times it is.
y-m-55-09.s.s3.hint.1: Write what value the product a×b must have for the difference to be 0.
y-m-55-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: When I put a=2, b=3 into the expression I wrote for the difference, do I get the difference of 12 seen above?
y-m-55-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the 'two rectangles' of the area model with the terms of the expression?
y-m-55-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that Daeun's expression is right in more cases than 'only when a and b are both 0'?
y-m-55-09.s.s3.model.0: If you expand (a+b)², you get a²+2ab+b², so the difference from a²+b² is 2ab. So Daeun's expression is right only when ab=0, that is, only when one of a and b is 0.
y-m-55-09.s.s3.model.1: When you divide the square, besides a×a and b×b there are 2 more a×b rectangles, so it gets bigger by 2×a×b. If a or b is 0, those pieces disappear, so they are equal only then.
y-m-55-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explained with the area model instead of expanding is also valid.

y-m-55-10.title: If we know only the sum, can we decide c?
y-m-55-10.topic: Roots and coefficients of a quadratic equation
y-m-55-10.goal: Check with examples that when only the sum of the two roots is known, the constant term of a quadratic equation is not decided as a single value, and give two different kinds of information needed to decide it as a single value.
y-m-55-10.material: b and c are integers, and the two roots p and q of the quadratic equation x²+bx+c=0 (x squared plus b times x plus c equals 0) are also integers (it is possible that p=q). The only thing known is the sum of the two roots, p+q=−5. We want to find the value of c.
y-m-55-10.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-55-10.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-55-10.prereq.0: The experience of meeting the relation b=−(p+q), c=pq when the quadratic expression x²+bx+c can be written in the form (x−p)(x−q) (middle school level)
y-m-55-10.prereq.2: Assignment note: 'H3' is only a mark of the difficulty and support level of this task set and does not determine in which high school grade it is learned. The high school Basic Math 1 track is regarded as a level of revisiting basic numbers, expressions, and equations, and the prerequisite learning below is assumed to have been learned already.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.prompt: With only the given information (the two roots are integers and their sum is −5), what can be said about the value of c?
y-m-55-10.s.s1.hint.0: Write the integer pairs with sum −5 in order, starting from −5.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write the product of each pair next to it and compare whether they are all the same.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.o.a: The roots are −2 and −3, so c is decided to be 6
y-m-55-10.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that recalled only one pair with sum −5 and took it as deciding the answer. Look for whether there are other pairs.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.o.b: The sum is −5, so c is decided to be 5
y-m-55-10.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that changed the sign of the sum and mixed up b and c. c is related to the product of the roots.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.o.c: We do not know b, so we cannot know c at all
y-m-55-10.s.s1.r.c: b is decided by the sum. What is unknown is not b but the product.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.o.d: c differs depending on the pair of roots, so it is not decided as a single value
y-m-55-10.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that made several possible pairs of roots and compared whether the products are the same.
y-m-55-10.s.s1.explain: The integer pairs with sum −5 are several, such as (−2, −3), (−1, −4), (0, −5), and their products are different, 6, 4, 0. So c is not decided as a single value.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 pairs of integers p, q with sum −5 whose products p×q are different values. (Pairs with the order swapped count as the same example.)
y-m-55-10.s.s2.hint.0: Decide one p so that the sum is −5 and fit q to it.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the product of the pair you chose and compare whether it is different from the products of the pairs already written.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are both integers.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make p and q both integers.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the two roots is −5.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.fail.c2: p+q is not −5. Check the sum again.
y-m-55-10.s.s2.explain: (−2, −3) has product 6, (−1, −4) has product 4, and (0, −5) has product 0. If the products differ, c differs too, so c cannot be decided from the sum alone.
y-m-55-10.s.s3.prompt: What more could we tell you in order to decide c as a single value? Write two different conditions, and also write what c becomes under each condition.
y-m-55-10.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one of the integer pairs with sum −5 and make a condition that points to only that pair, in one sentence.
y-m-55-10.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the product under that condition and write c.
y-m-55-10.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we tell you that one root is ..., then ...
y-m-55-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the two conditions I gave of different kinds?
y-m-55-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does the c found under each condition not conflict with the sum −5?
y-m-55-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is it not a condition that tells you the answer directly, like 'we tell you c'?
y-m-55-10.s.s3.model.0: If we tell you one of the two roots is −2, the other root is −3, so c=6. If we tell you the product of the two roots is 4, then c=4 right away.
y-m-55-10.s.s3.modelNote.0: A product condition gives c directly, so it is weak, but it is an allowed answer.
y-m-55-10.s.s3.model.1: If we say one root is 0, the other root is −5 and c=0. If we say the difference of the two roots is 1, they are −2 and −3, so c=6.
